name: Mazdutide
lead: Mazdutide (also IBI362 and LY3305677) is a once-weekly injectable peptide that activates both the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor and the glucagon receptor. It was developed by Innovent Biologics together with Eli Lilly, and received marketing approval in China in June 2025.[1]

In a phase 3 placebo-controlled trial in Chinese adults with obesity or overweight, once-weekly mazdutide was reported to produce clinically relevant weight loss versus placebo.[2] Earlier trials and a meta-analysis reported weight loss in people with and without diabetes.[5][4] It is a prescription drug in China and investigational elsewhere; it appears in looksmaxxing discussions as a possible next-generation fat-loss peptide.

Trial results give the clearest picture of the body-composition effect. In the phase 3 GLORY-1 trial of 610 Chinese adults, mean body weight at week 32 fell about 10 to 12.5 percent from baseline across the two mazdutide dose arms versus a 0.45 percent rise on placebo, and in the 60-week GLORY-2 trial of higher-dose mazdutide in adults with obesity the mean change was about -16.7 percent versus -1.5 percent on placebo.[2][19] The primary endpoints in these trials were total body weight and the share of participants losing at least 5 percent.

The point of interest for appearance is body composition: drugs in the GLP-1 family reduce appetite, and mazdutide adds glucagon-receptor activity that researchers have proposed raises energy expenditure, so it is discussed alongside semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide as a route to lower body fat.[1][11][3] Trial reports so far describe weight change as the main outcome and come mostly from Chinese populations.[2][5]

paras: Mazdutide has been studied for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity and for type 2 diabetes. A phase 3 trial randomised Chinese adults with a BMI of at least 28 (or overweight with other criteria) to mazdutide doses or placebo, and reported weight reduction with active treatment.[2] A phase 2 trial in Chinese adults with overweight or obesity ran 24 weeks of treatment up to 6 mg.[6]
In type 2 diabetes, a phase 2 trial evaluated mazdutide against placebo in adults managed with diet and exercise or stable metformin,[7] and a 2026 Nature report compared it with dulaglutide.[8]

According to the Drugs approval review, the first approval in June 2025 covers long-term weight management together with diet and physical activity in adults with a BMI of at least 28, or at least 24 with a weight-related condition; a second approval in September 2025 covers glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes, and the product is sold in China under the name Xinermei.[23] The same review notes the compound is under clinical evaluation for fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and alcohol use disorder.[23]

GLORY-1, a double-blind phase 3 trial in China published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025, randomised 610 adults (mean weight 87.2 kg, mean BMI 31.1) in equal groups to two mazdutide dose levels or placebo for 48 weeks. At week 32 the mean change in body weight was -10.09 percent and -12.55 percent in the two mazdutide groups versus +0.45 percent for placebo, and 73.9 percent and 82.0 percent of participants versus 10.5 percent on placebo lost at least 5 percent of body weight; the authors concluded that mazdutide produced clinically relevant weight reduction.[2]

The earlier phase 2 trial (248 adults randomised across three dose levels and placebo) reported mean 24-week weight changes of -6.7, -10.4 and -11.3 percent versus +1.0 percent on placebo, with diarrhoea, nausea and upper respiratory tract infection the most common adverse events.[6] GLORY-2, a 60-week phase 3 trial in 461 adults with a BMI of 30 or more (about 16 percent with type 2 diabetes, mean age 33.9), found a mean change of -16.65 percent on mazdutide versus -1.50 percent on placebo, a between-group difference of -15.15 percent, and reported more gastrointestinal adverse reactions on the drug than on placebo.[19]

A phase 1b trial reported up to 6.4% body weight loss over 12 weeks at doses up to 6 mg, and extended testing to 9 mg and 10 mg.[9] A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials has pooled mazdutide's effects on weight loss in diabetic and non-diabetic patients,[5] and network meta-analyses have placed it alongside other GLP-1 receptor agonists and polyagonists.[10] Most trial participants have been Chinese adults, so applicability to other populations has not been established in published trials.

Beyond weight, Nature reported 2026 phase 3 trials in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes, one against placebo and one against dulaglutide.[20][8] A phase 2 trial registered in 2023 as NCT06124807 compared LY3305677 with placebo in adults with obesity or overweight.[21] Because trial populations were Chinese adults, trial authors and reviewers have not established whether results transfer to other groups.[2][10]

Mazdutide belongs to the poly-agonist peptides, a group that Wikipedia lists with retatrutide, survodutide and tirzepatide.[1] It is described as an analogue of oxyntomodulin, a gut hormone that acts on both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, and its molecular formula is C210H322N46O67 with a molar mass of about 4563 g/mol.[1] Reviews of emerging obesity drugs place it with other combination incretin approaches that aim to add to the appetite effect of GLP-1 alone with an effect on energy use.[10][11]

Mazdutide combines GLP-1 receptor activation, which reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying, with glucagon receptor activation, which has been proposed to raise energy expenditure; it is described as an analogue of oxyntomodulin.[1][11][3]

In the 60-week GLORY-2 trial, participants on mazdutide reported more gastrointestinal adverse reactions than those on placebo, and the investigators described the treatment as providing clinically meaningful weight reduction despite this.[19] In the diabetes phase 3 comparison with dulaglutide in 731 participants, the incidence of gastrointestinal adverse events was higher with mazdutide while the drug was described as generally safe over 28 weeks.[8]

Published trials describe gastrointestinal effects typical of the GLP-1 class.[2][9] Readers should consult the primary trial reports for event rates; long-term safety data beyond the phase 3 programme remain limited.

Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics developed the compound, which has carried the names IBI362 and LY3305677. Phase 1b studies in Chinese adults were published in 2021 and 2022, including a 12-week multiple-ascending-dose study reporting weight loss of up to 6.4% at doses up to 6 mg and a follow-up study at 9 mg and 10 mg.[1][9] A phase 2 trial in Chinese adults with overweight or obesity followed in 2023,[6] and the phase 3 trial in Chinese adults with overweight or obesity was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in May 2025.[1][2] Mazdutide injection was approved for marketing in China in June 2025.[1] A 9 mg phase 3 trial, GLORY-2, was reported in JAMA in 2026.[19]
Mazdutide is approved only in China. Outside that market it is an investigational drug, and online discussions of it concern unapproved access. Specific sourcing is outside the scope of this wiki.

In looksmaxxing communities, mazdutide is mentioned as a newer relative of the GLP-1 drugs used for fat loss, particularly because it is approved in one country while remaining investigational elsewhere.[1] Wikipedia lists its legal status as prescription-only in China and investigational elsewhere.[1]

Because approval so far covers China alone and Lilly and Innovent describe the compound as investigational in other markets, mazdutide is discussed online mainly as a developing member of the GLP-1 and glucagon dual-agonist group rather than as a product with a defined route to purchase.[1][23]

Registered trials are exploring mazdutide in conditions including fatty pancreas, polycystic ovary syndrome, gout with obesity, type 1 diabetes, coronary plaque, mild cognitive impairment in type 2 diabetes, alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis-related portal hypertension.[12][13][14][15][16][17][18]
Registered studies also include a phase 3 trial in people with type 2 diabetes and early cognitive impairment (LIGHT-COG) and a phase 2 trial in alcohol use disorder.[22][17]

Human trials include a phase 3 trial in Chinese adults with obesity or overweight,[2] a phase 2 weight-loss trial,[6] a phase 1b multiple-ascending-dose trial,[9] a phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes,[7] and a comparison with dulaglutide.[8] A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled the weight-loss trials.[5]

In type 2 diabetes, the phase 3 trial against dulaglutide reported larger reductions in HbA1c (treatment differences of about -0.24 and -0.30 percentage points) and larger reductions in body weight (about 3.8 and 5.8 percent greater) with the two mazdutide dose levels over 28 weeks.[8] Trial populations have been Chinese adults.

card.summary: Weekly GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist approved in China for weight loss; strong trial data, but regional approval only.
card.note: Approved only in China; investigational elsewhere. Trials mostly in Chinese adults.

quick.overview:
Mazdutide is a once-weekly injection that activates both GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, developed by Innovent and Eli Lilly. It was approved for weight management in China in June 2025.

A phase 3 placebo-controlled trial in Chinese adults with obesity or overweight reported meaningful weight loss. Participants in most trials have been Chinese adults.
quick.mechanism: The GLP-1 component reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying; the glucagon component is proposed to increase energy expenditure.
quick.risks: Trials describe GI side effects typical of GLP-1 drugs. It is a prescription drug in China and investigational elsewhere, so use outside approved markets means unregulated supply.
